reason: Broken. The shipped wording is a splice of two different renderings and exists in neither. I read both papers the verifier leaned on. Lascano, “Émilie Du Châtelet on Illusions” (penultimate draft of JAPA 7.1, 2021), the very PDF the verifier gives as its URL, block quotes the whole passage at (2009: 349) and it reads: “In order to be happy, one must have freed oneself of PREJUDICE, one must be virtuous, healthy, have tastes and passions, and be susceptible to illusions; for we owe most of our pleasures to illusions, and unhappy is the one who has lost them.” Singular. Lascano, “Émilie du Châtelet's Theory of Happiness: Passions and Character”, quotes at (DH 349) only the first half, and that half reads “prejudices”, plural, stopping dead at “susceptible to illusions”. So the plural comes from the half quotation and the tail comes from the full one, and the verifier joined them. No published quotation of page 349 reads as this card would print it. That is minting wording by splice, which the standard forbids outright. The note also conceals the balance of evidence: it says “a second quotation of the same page prints prejudice in the singular”, as though the singular were the outlier, when the singular is the reading of the only full quotation of the sentence anyone has produced, and it is the very source the evidence field cites. The note's defence, that the French has préjugés in the plural, is exactly the reasoning this track bans: the card names a translation and must print that translator's wording, not a better guess at the French. I could not open the Chicago 2009 volume either: Internet Archive selectedphilosop0000duch is lending-only with search inside closed, both fulltext endpoints return “item not available”, the Google Books API is quota-blocked, and philarchive and jmphil.org sit behind Cloudflare and Anubis. So the page stays unopened and the line stays a hedge whatever wording it carries. If May wants it, it ships only in the reading that exists in print, singular “prejudice”, and only with a note saying plainly that the Chicago page was never opened and that the whole sentence has been found in exactly one scholarly quotation, a penultimate draft. My own recommendation is to drop it: with twenty carry-ins already on the table, May does not need a line whose single witness is a preprint.
